newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Howard sees lower Australia jobless over time.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Howard sees lower Australia jobless over time.

text.p: Australian Prime Minister John Howard said on Monday the unemployment rate would come down over time as long as his conservative government could free up the labour market and run a faster rate of economic growth.

"Unemployment will come down in this country if we can free the labour market and run a faster rate of economic growth without provoking a balance of payments crisis," Howard told Australian Broadcasting Corp radio.
"If we can do those two things, and all of our policies are directed to doing those two things, then over time unemployment will come down," he said.

Howard said previous attempts to speed up economic growth had failed because the stronger growth led to an import surge and a balance of payments crisis which prompted higher interest rates and which in turn increased the unemployment rate.
"You've got to try and break that cycle," he said.

Australia needed to increase its savings to ensure future growth and investment surges were not accompanied by a surge in imports. "We're addressing the savings problem through reducing the budget deficit," he said.

Howard said the government's plans to cut the budget deficit by A$7.2 billion over the next two years were not too fast as the economy had been growing for a long time and there was always the risk of an unexpected downturn in foreign growth rates.
The government forecast in its August 20 budget that the underlying budget deficit, which excludes asset sale proceeds, would be in surplus by 1998/99.

"We've now had three to four years of economic growth and we're still in deficit. Now heaven help us if through disadvantageous world economic circumstances, economic growth in Australia slowed down," he said.

"One of the things working for us is strong growth in America, reviving economic growth in Japan, strong economic growth continuing in the Asia Pacific region, but if those circumstances were to change through no fault of our own, we would be in a real pickle," he said.
Howard repeated that the government's forecast of unemployment staying at its current 8.5 percent on average through 1996/97 was cautious.
